title: Architecture Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance + ADRs
author: Jordan Ellis
body:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's architecture and engineering standards spanning API design, coding conventions, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, performance objectives, and the process for recording Architecture Decision Records (ADRs). It is intended as a canonical reference for engineers, SREs, and product teams when designing or changing services that participate in the inference platform.

Goals

- Reduce cognitive load and onboarding by standardizing common patterns.
- Enable predictable operational characteristics (latency, SLOs, cost).
- Make system behavior auditable and decisions discoverable via ADRs.
- Provide clear ownership and rollout/rollback practices for model-serving changes.

Scope

Applies to all services in the Redwood codebase and private deployments where Redwood components are deployed (hosted, dedicated, private). Exceptions require explicit approval via an ADR.

1) API Standards

Principles

- Keep public API contracts minimal and versioned. Use semantic versioning for public SDK endpoints and contract-level versioning for REST/JSON schemas.
- Prefer resource-oriented APIs (RESTful) for management/control plane and RPC/gRPC for high-throughput internal inference paths.
- All APIs must be documented in the central API registry (OpenAPI/Proto repository) and referenced from the service README.

Conventions

- Use OpenAPI v3 for REST endpoints; include examples and error schemas.
- Naming: kebab-case for REST paths (/v1/model-pools), snake_case for JSON keys in payloads, and PascalCase for enum values.
- Pagination: keyset-based pagination only for high-cardinality lists; otherwise use offset with size limits.
- Error model: top-level error object {code, message, details[]}. Map HTTP status codes to documented error codes.

Example: Error response JSON

{
  "error": {
    "code": "quota_exceeded",
    "message": "Request quota exceeded for route",
    "details": ["retry_after_seconds=30"]
  }
}

Versioning and Rollouts

- Backwards-incompatible changes require a new API version and an ADR describing the migration impact.
- Feature flags and per-account routing should be used for gradual rollouts of new routes.
- Deprecation: announce 90 days before removal for public endpoints, with automated usage metrics tracked.

Ownership and Documentation

- Each route must list an owning team in the route registry and a primary contact.
- OpenAPI specs must be included in the same repo as the service; automated linting via CI validates schema compatibility.

2) Coding Standards

Language & Style

- Use the company standard linters and formatters: gofmt/clang-format/black/prettier depending on language.
- Follow idiomatic patterns for each language; prefer simple, well-tested implementations over clever optimizations.

Repository Layout

- Services must include README, CONTRIBUTING, OWNERS, and an api/ directory for schema definitions.
- Tests: unit tests must cover core logic with minimum 60% coverage; critical path components (auth, routing, batching) must be covered above 85%.

Code Review

- Two approvers required for production-impacting PRs. One approver must be from the owning team, and at least one reviewer must be from a different team for cross-cutting changes.

Security and Secrets

- No secrets in code. Use KMS-backed environment variables or Vault. PR checks reject commits containing secret-like patterns.

3) Infrastructure Standards

Network and Accounts

- All cloud infrastructure must be provisioned via Terraform modules stored in the central terraform-and-iac repo. Manual changes are forbidden; exceptions require temporary exception ADR + documentation.
- VPC designs: private subnets for compute, public subnets for load balancers only. Inter-region traffic must use peering or private links with documented ACLs.

Compute and Scaling

- GPU-backed services are managed via the gpu-fleet-and-capacity guide; each pool must expose capacity metrics and per-tenant quotas.
- Use autoscaling policies tuned to request queue length and GPU utilization; prefer predictive scaling for periodic workloads.

Deployment Safety

- Canary deployments for all model-serving components with automated health checks. Default canary size: 5% traffic for 15 minutes with success criteria defined in rollout spec.

4) Model-Serving Standards

Model Packaging and Metadata

- Models must include a manifest.json with fields: model_id, framework, architecture, tokenizer, quantization_profile, required_memory_gb, input_dtype. (Example manifest below.)

Example manifest.json snippet:

{
  "model_id": "redwood/gptx-8b-v1",
  "framework": "pytorch",
  "architecture": "decoder-only",
  "tokenizer": "bpe",
  "quantization_profile": "q4_0",
  "required_memory_gb": "24",
  "input_dtype": "int32"
}

Serving Patterns

- Preferred runtime: Redwood Inference runtime vX+ (see runtime-architecture doc). Use sharded KV cache for long context workloads and continuous batching for small requests.
- Fallbacks: every serving route must declare one compatible fallback model version and a routing policy (latency-first | cost-first | availability-first).

Model Rollout Checklist (canary -> full):

1. Verify model unit tests and evals (latency, PPL, targeted prompts).
2. Deploy canary to dedicated canary pool: 5% traffic for 15 minutes.
3. Monitor SLOs and quality metrics; run automated prompt-set regressions.
4. If pass, increase to 25% for 1 hour; then 100% gradual shift.
5. If regression detected, automatic rollback to previous model by routing policy.

Quantization and Compatibility

- Approved quantization profiles are in quantization-profiles directory; use recommended profiles per architecture. Incompatible quantizations must have explicit ADRs.

5) Observability Standards

Metrics

- Metric names: dot-separated, low-cardinality labels only. Examples: inference.latency.p50_ms, inference.tokens_per_second, model.cache.hit_rate.
- Required metrics for every serving service: request_count, error_count, latency_p50, latency_p95, latency_p99, tokens_generated.

Tracing and Logs

- Distributed tracing with W3C trace-context headers is required for cross-service latency investigations. Sample rate: 1% by default; adjustable by service.
- Structured JSON logs with fields: timestamp, level, service, trace_id, span_id, request_id, message, attributes. Do not log PII.

Alerting and Dashboards

- SLO-based alerting: use burn rate alerts for SLO windows and a pager threshold for sustained incidents.
- Include a per-service dashboard with: SLO heatmap, latency histograms, error trends, and top slow routes.

6) Performance Standards and SLOs

Default SLOs (recommendations; adjust per product):

| Surface | SLI | SLO | Alert Threshold | Owner |
| - | - | - | - | - |
| Hosted inference (text generation) | p95 latency (ms) | <= 500 ms | p95 > 750 ms for 10m | eng-serving-runtime |
| Dedicated (reserved GPUs) | throughput (tokens/sec/pool) | within 90% of committed capacity | sustained < 85% for 30m | eng-sre |
| Model uploads and onboarding | success rate | 99.9% | < 99.5% per day | eng-platform |

Load-testing and Benchmarks

- All changes that affect hot paths must have benchmark results in benchmarking-and-perf-suite. Benchmarks must include: latency distribution, memory footprint, and token throughput for representative prompts.
- Use synthetic and replay-based benchmarks. Provide CLI to reproduce:

CLI example:

redwood-bench --target http://staging-inference:8080 --model redwood/gptx-8b-v1 --concurrency 64 --duration 300 --prompts prompts/testset.json

7) Decision Records (ADRs)

Purpose and Format

- All significant architectural decisions (protocol changes, quantization choices, new runtime kernels, public API breaking changes) must be captured as an ADR. ADRs make the rationale, alternatives, and consequences discoverable.

Required ADR fields: title, status (proposed|accepted|deprecated), date, authors, context, decision, consequences, rollback plan, related pages.

Process

1. Draft ADR as markdown in the service repo under docs/adrs/. File name: YYYYMMDD-title.md.
2. Assign reviewers from affected teams.
3. After approval, move the ADR to the canonical ADR registry in architecture-and-standards and set status=accepted.

Example ADR summary (short):

- Title: Use keyset pagination for model listing
- Status: accepted
- Date: 2026-01-15
- Decision: Adopt keyset pagination for model listing endpoints to avoid performance cliffs for large catalogs.

8) Governance and Ownership

- Architecture Steering: meet monthly to review high-impact ADRs, deprecations, and cross-cutting standards.
- Standards are living; proposed changes follow the ADR process and require an engineering steering OK and at least one external reviewer.

9) Runbook & Incident Guidance (summary)

- For production inference incidents: triage, run the standard inference incident playbook (oncall_and_incident_response/runbook). Key steps: identify failing pool, switch routing to fallback pool, reduce canary traffic, and open incident in status page.

Appendices

A. Model manifest canonical fields

- model_id, framework, architecture, tokenizer, quantization_profile, required_memory_gb, min_gpu_compute_sm, compatible_runtime_versions, recommended_batch_size

B. Standard rollout JSON example

{
  "rollout": {
    "strategy": "canary",
    "phases": [
      {"percent": 5, "duration_minutes": 15},
      {"percent": 25, "duration_minutes": 60},
      {"percent": 100, "duration_minutes": 120}
    ],
    "success_criteria": {"p95_latency_ms": 750, "error_rate": 0.01}
  }
}

C. Useful links

- Runtime architecture: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture
- Quantization profiles: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles
- ADR registry: /confluence/architecture-and-standards/adr-registry

If you have questions or need an exception for a specific workload, open an ADR draft and ping the Architecture Steering channel on Slack.
